title: The Canterbury Tales
description: Chaucer's unfinished masterpiece and the supreme achievement of Middle English literature: a frame-tale collection in which some thirty pilgrims journeying from the Tabard Inn to Canterbury agree to a storytelling contest, the tales ranging from the Knight's romance and the Miller's fabliau to the Wife of Bath's prologue, the Pardoner's sermon, and the Parson's treatise. Begun c. 1387 and left unfinished at Chaucer's death in 1400.
plot_or_argument: In the General Prologue the narrator joins a company of pilgrims — knight, miller, reeve, wife of Bath, pardoner, summoner, nun's priest, and the rest — each vividly portrayed; Harry Bailly, the Host, proposes the tale-telling game, and the tales that follow answer and quarrel with one another across the whole range of medieval genres, from courtly romance (Knight, Squire, Franklin) through fabliau (Miller, Reeve, Shipman, Merchant) and saint's life (Second Nun, Prioress) to sermon (Pardoner), beast fable (Nun's Priest), and the closing penitential treatise of the Parson.
narrative_structure: A frame narrative (the pilgrimage, the Host's game) enclosing twenty-four tales grouped into ten fragments; the links between tales stage the pilgrims' quarrels and judgments, and the work's unfinished state is part of its design.
principal_characters: the Narrator; the Host (Harry Bailly); the Knight; the Miller; the Reeve; the Wife of Bath; the Pardoner; the Friar; the Summoner; the Nun's Priest; the Parson; and the other pilgrims
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets of unprecedented flexibility, with rhyme royal, tail-rhyme, and prose for special effects; the decasyllabic line perfected.
historical_context: Composed c. 1387–1400 in London, drawing on Boccaccio, Ovid, Boethius, and the estates tradition; the pilgrimage to Becket's shrine at Canterbury supplied the frame; circulated in some eighty manuscripts and printed by Caxton (1476–78) and his successors, making it the foundation of the English printed canon.
literary_significance: The most influential single work of English literature: its pilgrims, its tales, and its frame established the English tradition of comic realism, dramatic monologue, and narrative irony that runs through Shakespeare to the novel.
attribution_notes: Uniquely well attested: Chaucer's authorship of the Tales is not in doubt, though the ordering of the fragments and some links are editorial.
bibliographical_notes: Some eighty manuscripts (Hengwrt, Ellesmere foremost). Standard edition: The Riverside Chaucer, ed. L. D. Benson (1987).

title: Troilus and Criseyde
description: Chaucer's great poem of love and loss, some 8,200 lines in rhyme royal, translating and transforming Boccaccio's Il Filostrato: the Trojan prince Troilus, aided by Pandarus, wins the love of Criseyde, loses her to the Greek camp in an exchange of prisoners, and learns of her betrayal with Diomede before his death in battle — all concluded by the narrator's Boethian repudiation of worldly love. The greatest love poem in Middle English.
plot_or_argument: Troilus, scorning love, is struck by Criseyde's beauty in the temple; his friend and uncle Pandarus engineers their union through letters and stratagems, and the lovers enjoy a secret happiness — until Criseyde is exchanged for the prisoner Antenor and sent to the Greek camp, where Diomede courts her and she yields; Troilus, after ominous dreams and the sight of the brooch he gave her on Diomede's armour, seeks death in battle, and his soul ascends to the eighth sphere, laughing at the woe of the world below.
narrative_structure: Five books moving from courtship through consummation to betrayal and death, framed by the narrator's ironic service to the servants of love and closed by the palinode commending the love of God.
principal_characters: Troilus; Criseyde; Pandarus; Diomede; Hector; the Narrator
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal stanzas (seven-line, ababbcc) handled with supreme flexibility; the first sustained masterpiece of the English decasyllabic line.
historical_context: Composed c. 1382–86 in London, after Chaucer's Italian journeys, adapting Boccaccio's Filostrato with additions from Boethius, Dante, and the Trojan romances; dedicated to 'moral Gower and philosophical Strode'; preserved in sixteen manuscripts and printed by Caxton (c. 1483).
literary_significance: The greatest narrative poem of the English Middle Ages after the Canterbury Tales; its psychological depth and tragic irony made it the model for Henryson's Testament of Cresseid and the ancestor of Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida.
attribution_notes: Chaucer's authorship secure; the work is the first he names in the Retraction.
bibliographical_notes: Sixteen manuscripts. Standard edition: The Riverside Chaucer (1987); B. A. Windeatt (1984).

title: The Book of the Duchess
alternative_titles: The Deth of Blaunche the Duchesse
description: Chaucer's earliest major poem (1,334 lines in octosyllabic couplets), a dream vision elegy for Blanche, Duchess of Lancaster, who died in 1368: the insomniac dreamer overhears a grieving knight in black, whose lament for his lost lady — 'White' — unfolds the ideal of courtly love into a meditation on death and consolation. The poem that founded the English dream-vision tradition.
plot_or_argument: The dreamer, sleepless from an eight-year love-sickness, reads Ovid's tale of Ceyx and Alcyone and falls asleep; in his dream he meets the Man in Black, who tells of his long service to Fortune and of the peerless lady White whom he won and has now lost; only the dreamer's blunt question — 'she is dead?' — breaks the elegy's obliqueness, and the dream ends with the hunting of the hart and the poem's closure on the word 'king'.
narrative_structure: A double frame (reading; dream) enclosing the knight's elegiac autobiography, in the French dit manner; the wordplay on 'White', 'hart/heart', and 'king' ties consolation to allegory.
principal_characters: the Dreamer; the Man in Black; Lady White; Fortune
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic couplets of courtly grace, adapted from Machaut and the Roman de la Rose.
historical_context: Composed c. 1368–72, commemorating Blanche of Lancaster (d. 12 September 1368), first wife of John of Gaunt, Chaucer's patron; the poem's courtly audience would have recognized the dead duchess in the knight's 'White'.
literary_significance: The first great English dream poem and the foundation of Chaucer's mature art; its fusion of consolation, allegory, and courtly elegy shaped the entire English dream-vision tradition.
attribution_notes: Chaucer's authorship secure; the occasional reference to Blanche is universally accepted.
bibliographical_notes: Three manuscripts. Standard edition: The Riverside Chaucer (1987).

title: The House of Fame
description: Chaucer's comic dream vision of fame and rumour (2,158 lines in octosyllabic couplets, unfinished): the dreamer is carried by a talkative eagle through the heavens to the House of Fame, where the goddess dispenses reputation with sublime arbitrariness, and on to the whirling House of Rumour where every report, true and false, takes wing. A poem about poetry, authority, and the instability of language itself.
plot_or_argument: The dreamer, pondering the causes of dreams and the nature of fame, finds himself in a temple of Venus adorned with the story of the Aeneid; an eagle (comically garrulous, in the Dantean manner) snatches him up and lectures him on sound, air, and the physics of speech; before the House of Fame he sees the petitioners — great and small — receive arbitrary reward or oblivion; and in the twig-built, whirling House of Rumour every tiding breeds and flies; the poem breaks off as 'a man of gret auctorite' appears.
narrative_structure: Three movements (the temple of Venus; the eagle's flight and lecture; the houses of Fame and Rumour), with the Aeneid and the physics of sound as its digressive armature.
principal_characters: the Dreamer (Geffrey); the Eagle; Fame; Aeolus; the suitors of Fame; the 'man of great authority'
meter_and_prosody: Octosyllabic couplets with colloquial verve; the eagle's lecture burlesques the didactic mode.
historical_context: Composed c. 1378–80, during Chaucer's Italian-inspired middle period, drawing on Dante, Virgil, Ovid, and Boethius; the invocation promises tidings 'of love or such thinges glade' — a tease never fulfilled.
literary_significance: The most brilliant medieval English poem about poetry, fame, and the circulation of language; its self-reflexive comedy anticipates the metacritical concerns of modern literature.
bibliographical_notes: Three manuscripts. Standard edition: The Riverside Chaucer (1987).

title: The Parliament of Fowls
description: Chaucer's St Valentine's Day dream vision (699 lines in rhyme royal): guided by Scipio's dream and the gate's ambiguous inscription, the dreamer enters the garden of love, where Nature presides over the parliament of birds choosing their mates on the feast of Venus. The debate between the noble eagles and the commons of birds is the great medieval comedy of class, desire, and natural law.
plot_or_argument: After reading Cicero's Somnium Scipionis, the dreamer is led by Africanus through the gate ('through me men go to that blessed place' / 'through me the way to sorrow') into Nature's park, where the goddess holds the parliament of fowls; three aristocratic eagles court the formel on her wrist, their courtly pleas answered by the lower birds' impatient cry 'have done, and let us wende!' — and the formel's request for a year's delay leaves the parliament, and the poem, in unresolved suspension.
narrative_structure: A tripartite vision (reading and gate; the garden and temple; the parliament and debate), with the roundel of summer as its lyric centre.
principal_characters: the Dreamer; Africanus; Nature; the three eagles; the formel; the goose, cuckoo, turtledove, and other birds
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal stanzas, with the lyric roundel ('Now welcom somer') inset.
historical_context: Composed c. 1380–82, traditionally read against the marriage negotiations of Richard II (to Anne of Bohemia, 1382); the Valentine convention and the bird parliament derive from French and Italian love vision.
literary_significance: The classic English poem of Valentine's Day and the finest medieval treatment of the bird parliament; its satire of courtly and common 'commune profyt' is a touchstone of Chaucer's political art.
bibliographical_notes: Fourteen manuscripts. Standard edition: The Riverside Chaucer (1987).

title: The Legend of Good Women
description: Chaucer's unfinished collection of exemplary women's legends (some 2,700 lines), framed by the Prologue in which the god of Love arraigns the poet for slandering women and his queen Alceste assigns him the penance of commemorating good women betrayed by men. Its nine completed legends — Cleopatra, Thisbe, Dido, Hypsipyle and Medea, Lucrece, Ariadne, Philomela, Phyllis, and Hypermnestra — are the seedbed of the English legendary tradition.
plot_or_argument: The Prologue stages the daisy-worship of the poet and his dream trial before the god of Love, who condemns him for the Troilus and the Romaunt; Alceste's intercession wins him the commission to write of faithful women and false men. The legends that follow retell the classical stories of love and betrayal in rhyme royal, until the collection breaks off, unfinished, in the legend of Hypermnestra.
narrative_structure: A dream-vision prologue (two versions, F and G) framing a series of Ovidian legends, each structured as betrayal narrative with moral close.
principal_characters: the Narrator; the god of Love; Alceste; Cleopatra; Thisbe; Dido; Medea; Lucrece; Ariadne; Philomela; Phyllis; Hypermnestra
meter_and_prosody: Rhyme royal, with the prologue in heroic couplets in the G version.
historical_context: Composed c. 1386–88, partly at the queen's (Anne of Bohemia's) request, during the period of the Canterbury Tales' beginnings; its Prologue is the richest single document of Chaucer's self-presentation as poet.
literary_significance: The founding text of the English 'good women' tradition (Bokenham's Legends, the Tudor mirrors) and a key witness to Chaucer's negotiation with the courtly politics of gender.
attribution_notes: Chaucer's authorship secure; the relationship of the two prologues is editorial.
bibliographical_notes: Twelve manuscripts. Standard edition: The Riverside Chaucer (1987).

title: Treatise on the Astrolabe
description: Chaucer's prose treatise on the construction and use of the astrolabe, written in 1391 for his ten-year-old son Lewis: the first technical treatise in English prose, and the earliest English work on a scientific instrument. Its precision, clarity, and fatherly address make it unique in the medieval English canon.
plot_or_argument: In five planned parts — of which the first two and a supplement survive — the treatise describes the astrolabe and its parts, teaches the child to take altitudes and tell the time, and promises the tables and theories that would complete the work; the famous prologue addresses 'Lyte Lowys my sone' with pedagogical tenderness.
narrative_structure: A didactic treatise of definitions, propositions, and conclusions, each numbered for the child's use, with worked examples from the Oxford latitude.
meter_and_prosody: Prose: plain, exact, and carefully ordered, in the tradition of the practical manual.
historical_context: Dated 1391 in the prologue, written for Lewis Chaucer, then about ten years old, in London; it draws on the Latin tradition of Messahala and the practical astronomy of the universities; preserved in some thirty manuscripts.
literary_significance: The first scientific prose in English and the classic of its kind: the treatise's plain style is a landmark in the development of English as a language of learning.
attribution_notes: Chaucer's authorship secure (named in the prologue).
bibliographical_notes: Some thirty manuscripts. Standard edition: The Riverside Chaucer (1987).

title: Boece
description: Chaucer's prose translation of Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, the work that above all others shaped his thought: the dialogue between the imprisoned Boethius and Lady Philosophy on fortune, free will, providence, and the sovereign good. Made c. 1380–86 with the aid of the commentary tradition, it is the foundation of the Boethian strain that runs through all his poetry.
plot_or_argument: Boethius, imprisoned and awaiting death, laments his fall until Lady Philosophy appears and, through a graduated argument in prose and verse (the metres), cures him: showing that fortune is mutable by nature, that true happiness lies in God, that evil men are punished by their own wickedness, and that providence and free will are compatible.
narrative_structure: Five books of alternating prose and metrical sections, in the Menippean form of the original; Chaucer renders the metres in prose, with explanatory glosses from the commentaries.
meter_and_prosody: Prose translation of the whole, metres included, dense with the philosophical vocabulary Chaucer coined or naturalized.
historical_context: Composed c. 1380–86, drawing on the Latin text and the commentary of Nicholas Trevet; its influence pervades Chaucer's mature poems (Troilus, the Knight's Tale, the ballades) and the whole English Boethian tradition.
literary_significance: The most consequential translation Chaucer made: through it, the Consolation became English literature's native philosophical idiom, from Chaucer to Elizabeth I's translation and beyond.
attribution_notes: Chaucer's authorship secure (named in the Retraction).
bibliographical_notes: Nine manuscripts. Standard edition: The Riverside Chaucer (1987).

title: The Romaunt of the Rose
description: A Middle English translation of the Roman de la Rose, surviving in a single manuscript and divided by scholarship into three fragments (A, B, and C), of which only Fragment A is now widely accepted as Chaucer's — and even that attribution is debated. The work is the great conduit by which the French allegory of love entered English, and its early attribution to Chaucer long shaped the poet's canon.
plot_or_argument: The dreamer enters the garden of Mirth, where the god of Love shoots him and he pledges service; the narrative then follows the lover's quest for the Rose through the allegorical figures of the garden — Fair Welcome, Danger, Reason, Shame, Jealousy — in the French poem's anatomy of courtly love.
narrative_structure: A continuous allegorical dream vision following the French original's sequence of episodes, surviving here in three discontinuous fragments.
principal_characters: the Dreamer-Lover; the Rose; the god of Love; Fair Welcome; Danger; Reason; Jealousy; the Old Woman
historical_context: Composed in the 1360s–70s (Fragment A possibly c. 1360s), translating Guillaume de Lorris and Jean de Meun; preserved uniquely in the Hunterian manuscript (Glasgow, Hunter 409); the attribution to Chaucer rests on his own mention of a Romaunt translation in the Legend of Good Women prologue and on Thynne's 1532 edition.
literary_significance: The principal English version of the poem that dominated late medieval literary culture; the attribution question remains a central problem of Chaucerian scholarship.
attribution_notes: Authorship disputed: Fragment A is often accepted as Chaucer's; Fragments B and C are generally rejected; modern editors treat the whole as doubtful. authorship_status reflects this uncertainty.
bibliographical_notes: Glasgow, Hunterian MS 409. Standard edition: The Riverside Chaucer (1987, as doubtful).

title: Chaucer's Short Poems
alternative_titles: The Minor Poems of Geoffrey Chaucer
description: The corpus of Chaucer's shorter poems: the philosophical ballades (Fortune, Truth, Gentilesse, Lak of Stedfastnesse), the complaints (Anelida and Arcite, the Complaint of Mars, the Complaint unto Pity, A Complaint to his Lady), the envoy to Scogan, the ABC to the Virgin, and the love lyrics. Together they show the courtly poet at work across every register, from the rueful 'Flee fro the prees' to the burlesque of Sir Thopas's kin.
plot_or_argument: The poems range from the lover's complaints of Mars and Anelida (with its paired verse of great formal ambition) through the moral ballades on truth and steadfastness — 'Flee fro the prees, and dwelle with sothfastnesse' — to the devotional ABC and the comic self-portraits of the envoys.
narrative_structure: A corpus of independent lyrics and complaints, several (Anelida and Arcite, the Complaint of Mars) with substantial narrative frames.
principal_characters: the speakers of the complaints and ballades; Mars; Venus; Anelida; Arcite
meter_and_prosody: Ballades, roundels, rhyme royal, and experimental stanzas; the ABC is an alphabetical acrostic in translation from Deguileville.
historical_context: Composed across Chaucer's career (c. 1370–1400), many for courtly occasions and patrons (John of Gaunt, the king's circle); preserved in the manuscript anthologies of the fifteenth century and collected by Thynne (1532).
literary_significance: The ballade of Truth and its kin made Chaucer the English master of the short moral poem; the corpus preserves the courtly occasions and formal experiments of his art.
attribution_notes: The core canon is secure; a few attributions remain debated.
bibliographical_notes: Many manuscripts. Standard edition: The Riverside Chaucer (1987).
